All agree that "majesty and honour" denote God's greatness, self-sufficiency and generosity towards His friends, and that "Face" refers to His Essence, though they differ on the detail: al-Razi and al-Qurtubi take it to be the Being itself, al-Zamakhshari treats it as a figurative expression for the Essence, and Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Uthaymin affirm the attribute of a Face without likening it to created faces.

Most exegetes hold that "Whoever is in the heavens and earth asks Him" means that all creation depends on Him for provision, forgiveness, life and death. Al-Tabari reports from Mujahid and 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr that "every day He is in some affair" means He answers the one who calls, relieves the distressed and heals the sick; al-Razi and al-Baghawi explain this affair as giving life and death, provision, and raising or humbling people. A hadith transmitted through Abu al-Darda' says it includes forgiving sins, relieving distress, raising some peoples and lowering others; Ibn Kathir notes that al-Bukhari transmits it only as Abu al-Darda's own words.

Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Qurtubi note that the reading of Ibn Mas'ud and Ubayy, "dhi al-jalal", makes the phrase an attribute of the Lord rather than of the Face.

This verse states that everyone in the heavens and on earth, angels, humans and jinn alike, depends on God and asks Him for their needs, and none can do without Him. The commentators explain that "every day He is in some affair" means that God continually acts upon His creation in renewed ways: He gives life and causes death, bestows and withholds, raises and lowers, answers the caller, gives to the petitioner, relieves the distressed and heals the sick. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi note that the asking is both by speech, for those who speak, and by the state of need, for every creature. Many cite a hadith transmitted through Abu al-Darda', that this affair is to forgive a sin, relieve a distress, raise some peoples and lower others; al-Tabari, al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Kathir report it, while Ibn Kathir notes that it is also transmitted as Abu al-Darda's own words and its chain is debated. Al-Hasan ibn al-Fadl, reported by Ibn al-Jawzi, al-Razi and al-Qurtubi, holds that these are manifestations that God brings forth, not new initiatives: his eternal decree unfolds at its appointed time. Al-Razi offers several philosophical accounts of how divine action relates to change. Al-Baghawi and al-Nasafi report Ibn Abbas distinguishing the asking of the inhabitants of heaven, who seek forgiveness, from that of the inhabitants of earth, who seek provision and forgiveness. Al-Mawardi and Ibn Kathir mention the reading that the day divides into the day of worldly life, a time of trial, and the Day of Resurrection, a time of reckoning. Al-Baghawi reports that the verse was revealed in response to Jews who claimed God does not decree anything on Saturday. Most commentators read the verse as a statement of God's constant providence and the universal dependence of creation on Him.

The commentators explain that this verse, repeated through the surah after each favour, states that everyone on earth, whether human or jinn, is perishing, and that only the Face of your Lord, full of majesty and bounty, remains. The next verse adds that all who are in the heavens and on earth ask Him for what they need, whether by speech or by the state of their being, and that none can do without Him. The commentators agree that the phrase every day He is in some affair means that He acts at every moment: giving life and death, enriching and impoverishing, raising and lowering, answering the caller, relieving distress and forgiving sins. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir report such explanations from Mujahid, Ubayd ibn Umayr and Qatada, and reports traced to the Prophet, which Ibn Kathir treats as weak or disputed, give examples of these affairs. On the meaning of day, Ibn 'Uyayna distinguishes two days: the life of this world, where the affair is command, prohibition, life and death, and the Day of Resurrection, where it is recompense and reckoning. Others, al-Tabari among them, take it simply as each day of this world. Al-Razi reports that some understand the affair as the bringing of destinies to their appointed times, and that these are affairs He manifests rather than new affairs He begins. The phrase We shall attend to you, O two burdens, is taken by al-Baghawi and Ibn 'Atiyya as a figure of speech, since God is never occupied; it is a warning of the time of judgment, as one says to another, I will surely deal with you. Ibn Abbas and al-Dahhak read it as a challenge. The passage on flames and molten brass is discussed by al-Shawkani and Ibn 'Atiyya, who note several possible meanings of shiwaz and nuhas. The repeated refrain, according to the commentators, recalls the favours, including the warning itself.

God threatens jinn and humans that He will devote Himself to reckoning with them and repaying them. The word "free myself" does not mean that He is busy with a task that will end, since no affair distracts Him from another; it is a threat expressing the intent to requite. Ibn Abbas and al-Dahhak take it as a warning from God to His servants, while al-Kisa'i, al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj read it as an expression of intent to call them to account. Al-Hasan, Muqatil and Ibn Zayd understand it as the fulfilment of what God promised to the pious and threatened for the wicked. The "two weighty ones" are humans and jinn, and commentators give several reasons for the name: their weight upon the earth, their burden of sins according to Ja'far al-Sadiq, or the seriousness of their responsibility. On the phrase about passing beyond the regions of the heavens and earth, Ibn Abbas takes it to mean knowing what they contain, al-Dahhak to mean fleeing death, and al-Tabari, followed by others, places it on the Day of Resurrection when the angels surround the earth. On the word authority (sultan), Mujahid and Ibn Abbas understand proof or dominion, while Qatada takes it as kingship. The commentators agree that the verse establishes the helplessness of creatures before their Creator, and the passage ends by repeating the rebuke question.

This verse, according to the commentators, is a threat from God addressed to both jinn and humans, who will be called to account for their deeds. The most widely shared meaning is that God will turn to reckon with and recompense the two communities, rewarding those who obey and punishing those who disobey. The verse closes by reminding them of the blessings of God that they deny, a phrase repeated throughout the surah.

The exegetes agree that this 'leisure' attributed to God does not mean that He is occupied and then becomes free, since He is exempt from any preoccupation. Ibn Abbas, al-Dahhak and Ibn Kathir read it as a divine warning to the servants; al-Zajjaj, al-Kisa'i, Ibn al-Anbari and al-Qurtubi understand the verb as 'to set out toward', meaning: We will call you to account. Al-Hasan, Muqatil and Ibn Zayd connect the phrase to the fulfilment of the promises of reward and punishment.

As for the words 'O assembly of jinn and humans, if you are able to pass through the regions of the heavens and the earth, then pass through them', several readings are reported. Ibn Abbas takes it to mean knowing what is in the heavens and the earth, al-Dahhak as fleeing from death, and al-Tabari, citing Ibn Jarir, as a statement addressed on the Day of Resurrection when the angels encircle creation. The term 'sultan' is read by Mujahid as proof, by Qatada as royal power, and al-Tabari retains the sense of proof and evidence.

The commentators also differ on the 'shuwaz' and the 'nuhas': Ibn Abbas sees in the shuwaz pure flame, Mujahid a greenish intermittent flame, al-Dahhak a smoke rising from the flame; for the nuhas, Ibn Abbas and Sa'id ibn Jubayr see smoke, while Mujahid and Qatada see molten copper poured over their heads.

In this verse God addresses the jinn and humankind on the Day of Judgment, telling them that if they can pass through the regions of the heavens and the earth, they should try, but they will not be able to do so except by a power they do not possess. The commentators agree that the verse is one of challenge and warning, and that the "leisure" mentioned just before does not mean God is ever occupied; it means He will give His full attention to reckoning and requiting them. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi report that sultan here means power, dominion or authority, while Mujahid and others read it as proof or argument, and al-Tabari considers this second meaning closest to Arabic usage. Al-Dahhak holds that the passage describes people and jinn fleeing when the angels encircle creation on the Day of Resurrection, while others, such as Ibn Abbas in one report, understand it as fleeing death or seeking knowledge of what is in the heavens and the earth. On the flame and the molten brass, the views differ: shuwaz is for Ibn Abbas pure flame, for Mujahid a greenish broken flame, and for al-Dahhak smoke coming from the fire; nuhas is for Ibn Abbas and Sa'id ibn Jubayr smoke without flame, and for Mujahid and Qatada molten brass poured over their heads. The exegetes cite these opinions without ruling between them, the shared point being that whoever tries to escape will be driven back by punishment and will have no one to help him.

In this verse God addresses the jinn and humankind after warning them of the reckoning, declaring that they cannot escape His decree. The refrain repeated throughout the surah asks which of your Lord's blessings you deny. Commentators differ on when this address takes place. Ibn 'Abbas, al-Dahhak, Mujahid and Ibn Kathir understand it as the Day of Resurrection, when the angels surround creation from every direction and those who try to flee find no exit. Another report from Ibn 'Abbas, followed by 'Ata', reads it as a call to knowledge: if you can grasp what is in the heavens and the earth, grasp it, but you can only do so through a proof from God. Al-Dahhak also takes it as fleeing from death, which no one can avert. The meaning of sultan is likewise debated. Ibn 'Abbas and Qatada take it to mean kingship or God's authority, while Mujahid, 'Ikrima and al-Tabari take it as proof or argument, al-Tabari judging this the more usual sense in Arabic. As for shuwaz and nuhas, Ibn 'Abbas holds that shuwaz is pure flame and nuhas is smoke, whereas Mujahid and Qatada take nuhas to be molten copper poured over their heads. The verse thus affirms that no creature can escape God's judgement, with a threat of fiery punishment.

This verse says that on the Day of Judgment a flame of pure fire, called shuwaz, and nuhas will be sent down upon jinn and humans, and they will have no means of defending themselves against it. Ibn 'Abbas, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, al-Tabari, al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Kathir all take shuwaz to be a pure flame without smoke, while Mujahid describes it as a greenish, broken flame and al-Dahhak as smoke rising from the blaze. As for nuhas, Ibn 'Abbas, Sa'id ibn Jubayr and al-Tabari understand it as smoke without flame, citing a verse of al-Nabigha al-Ja'di, whereas Mujahid, Qatada and Ibn Mas'ud take it to be molten copper or dregs poured over their heads. Al-Tabari prefers the smoke reading, because a threat of pure fire should be followed by a punishment of the same kind. Ibn al-Qayyim, Ibn Kathir and Ibn Ashur link the verse to the scene of the gathering, where the angels surround creation and fugitives are driven back by fire. In terms of recitation, Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read nuhasin in the genitive as a continuation of nar, while the other readers use the nominative as a continuation of shuwaz. Al-Razi and al-Qurtubi discuss how the grammar works and note that the chouwaz may be a mixture of fire and smoke. Nearly all agree that the verse means no one can escape or be defended.

In this verse God addresses jinn and humankind after reminding them of His vast power and of their inability to escape Him. He tells them that a pure flame and a molten substance will be sent upon them, and that neither of them will be able to defend itself. The commentators differ on the meaning of shuwaz: Ibn Abbas, 'Ata' and others take it as a flame without smoke, Mujahid as a greenish, broken flame, and al-Dahhak as the smoke that rises from the flame; Abu 'Amr combined these by saying it means both fire and smoke. For nuhas, Ibn Abbas, Sa'id ibn Jubayr and most philologists, including al-Farra' and Abu 'Ubayda, understand smoke without flame, citing a line of al-Nabigha al-Ja'di; al-Tabari prefers this view, reasoning that a punishment by pure fire should be followed by something of the same kind. Mujahid and Qatada take it as molten brass poured over the heads, Ibn Mas'ud as dregs-like boiling liquid, and al-Dahhak as the sediment of boiling oil. The readings vary in the vowels of shuwaz and nuhas, all of which are transmitted. Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Razi stress that the verse conveys both threat and helplessness: you will be unable to escape or to be helped. As in the preceding verses, it closes with the refrain: which of your Lord's favours will you then deny?

This verse describes the sky on the Day of Resurrection: when it splits open, it becomes red like a rose and melts like oil or its dregs, under the terror of that day. The commentators agree that the splitting happens on the Last Day and that its colour changes, the affair becoming very grave. They differ on the meaning of "warda" (rose) and "dihan". Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir report that many took it to mean the colour of a "ward" horse, whose coat changes with the seasons, while Ibn Abbas, Abu Salih, al-Dahhak and al-Kalbi said it means red leather, and al-Farra' also used the horse image. Qatada and Sa'id ibn Jubayr understood plain redness, Qatada adding that the sky is green today. For "dihan", Mujahid, al-Dahhak and al-Farra' take it as the plural of "duhn", oil, pointing to the variety of its colours; al-Zamakhshari gives the sense of oil dregs, while Ibn Abbas links it to red leather. Al-Tabari judges the oil sense more correct for its brightness. Ibn Kathir and al-Mawardi describe the sky melting like molten metal. The commentators link this passage to the next statement that humans and jinn will not be questioned about their sins: Hasan and Qatada see different stages of that day, and Ibn Abbas separates the questioning meant to establish facts from the questioning meant to rebuke. The verse then returns to the two species, humans and jinn, to remind them of God's favours.

This passage of Surat ar-Rahman describes the terror of the Day of Resurrection, when the sky splits and turns red like a rose or like oil, one of the greatest horrors of that day. The commentators differ on the two images. Ibn 'Abbas, Abu Salih, al-Dahhak and al-Farra' understand the 'rose' as the colour of a dappled red horse that changes hue with the seasons, while Qatada, Sa'id ibn Jubayr and al-Zajjaj take it as the pure red of a rose. As for 'ad-dihan', al-Dahhak, Mujahid and al-Tabari link it to the word 'dihn', meaning oil or its purity, or to the sediment of oil, whereas Ibn 'Abbas, al-Kalbi and al-A'sha understand a red leather hide. Ibn 'Atiyya and Ibn al-Jawzi report that the sky melts and changes colour until it resembles melted oil. All agree that this splitting will take place on the Day of Resurrection. They differ over the following statement that no one will be questioned about his sin: al-Hasan and Qatada say the guilty are recognised by their marks, while Ibn 'Abbas explains that it is a questioning of rebuke rather than a search for information, and Ikrima distinguishes between different stages of that day. The refrain, 'Which of the bounties of your Lord will you deny?', is understood as a reminder of God's favours, including the warning and justice it announces.

This verse states that on the Day of Judgment, neither humans nor jinn will be asked about their sins in the sense of seeking information, because God has recorded and preserved them and knows them better than they do. They will instead be questioned in order to be rebuked and confounded. The commentators explain that the negation refers to the questioning that seeks knowledge, while the questioning that rebukes is affirmed in other verses, such as: By your Lord, We will surely question them all. Ibn 'Abbas holds that wherever questioning is mentioned it is for reproach, and wherever it is denied it is pure inquiry. Qatada and 'Ikrima say the Day has many stations, so in some they are questioned and in others they are not. Qatada also reports that there was questioning, then mouths were sealed and hands and feet spoke of what they had done. Mujahid says the angels do not question the criminals, who are recognised by their marks, namely blackened faces and bluish eyes, as al-Hasan explains. Al-Tabari holds that the angels do not question the wrongdoers about their sins, because God kept account of them. Al-Razi and al-Qurtubi discuss whether the pronoun refers to humans, meaning that no sinner is asked about his own sin. The passage belongs to a description of the terrors of the Last Day, and it closes with a reminder to both groups of the favours of God.

The commentators explain that this verse belongs to the description of the Day of Resurrection: neither humans nor jinn will be questioned about their sins in order to learn the facts, since God has recorded and preserved them. The guilty will be recognised by their marks, and then they will be told, in rebuke: "Which of the bounties of your Lord will you deny?" Al-Tabari sees in this God's justice, who punishes only the guilty. Al-Tabari, Mujahid, Qatada and al-Hasan hold that the angels do not question the criminals, who are known by blackened faces and blue eyes. Ibn Abbas, al-Tabari and others say the negated question is the question of inquiry, while the question of reproach remains. Ibn Kathir, Ibn al-Qayyim, al-Razi and Ibn Ashur reconcile this negation with verses describing questioning by holding that the Day has several stages. Al-Razi and al-Qurtubi understand that no one can plead for another, and Ibn Kathir, al-Baydawi and Abu al-Su'ud read the meaning as a prohibition of excuses. All agree that these reproaches come before the seizing by forelock and feet and the casting into Hell. Few commentators cite specific hadiths for this passage, apart from the report from 'A'isha cited by Ibn Kathir, whom he judges weak.

This verse states that on the Day of Resurrection the criminals will be recognised by their marks and then seized by the angels by their forelocks and feet and cast into the Fire. The commentators agree that the mark is blackness of the faces and blueness of the eyes, as al-Hasan al-Basri and Qatada said, and that the criminals here are the disbelievers and polytheists. They differ on how the seizing happens. Ibn Abbas, al-Dahhak and Muqatil hold that the guards bind the forelock and the feet together behind the back and throw the sinner into the Fire, while al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi and Ibn Juzayy say they are dragged, some seized by the forelock and others by the feet. Ibn Kathir notes that a report from Aisha on this point is a strange hadith that cannot be relied upon. The criminals are then rebuked: this is the Hellfire you used to deny. They move between it and a scalding water, which Qatada, Mujahid and Ibn Abbas understand as water whose heat has reached its extreme; Ka'b al-Ahbar describes it as a valley of Hell where the pus of its people gathers. The verse ends with the refrain, 'Which of your Lord's bounties will you deny?' The commentators explain this bounty in different ways. Most see it in the warning, which restrains from sin and encourages obedience, while al-Tabari sees it in the distinction made between the criminals and the obedient believers, so that only the former are humiliated.

This verse is a refrain that returns after the description of the criminals who are recognised by their marks and seized by their forelocks and feet to be thrown into the Fire. It asks jinn and humans which of their Lord's blessings they deny. The commentators agree that these blessings include the warnings and terrors themselves, since they restrain people from sin and guide them to obedience, as Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi explain. Al-Tabari adds that God's justice is itself a blessing, since He punishes only the guilty, while al-Zamakhshari sees the blessing in the deliverance of those who are saved. Ibn Uthaymin and al-Qasimi link the punishment of the disbelievers with the honour given to the believers. Al-Shawkani notes that death is a blessing because it transfers people to the abode of reward, and Abu Hayyan and Ibn Sa'di stress that the threat is itself a mercy. On the marks, al-Hasan and Qatada understand them as blackened faces and blue eyes, while others read them more broadly as humiliation or sorrow. On how they are seized, Ibn Abbas reports that they are gathered and thrown like firewood, al-Dahhak that the forelock and feet are bound together in a chain behind the back, and others that they are dragged. As for the boiling water described as ana, some take it to mean water whose heat has reached its limit, others a valley of Hell where the pus of the damned gathers, and others take it to mean present.

This verse is addressed to the criminals, who are told, as a rebuke and reproach, when they see Hell: this is the Fire you used to deny. The commentators see it as a moment of confrontation with what had once been dismissed. The next verse describes them circulating between the Fire and a boiling water, hamim ani. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, al-Dahhak and al-Hasan take ani to mean that its heat has reached its utmost limit. Ibn Zayd and a report from Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi understand it as meaning present, and Ibn Kathir also records that the water is simply extremely hot.

The commentators agree that the damned are tormented in the blaze and given this drink to drink in turn. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi and Ibn Sa'di present it this way, and Ibn Kathir adds that it tears apart the bowels. Al-Baghawi and Ibn al-Jawzi transmit Ka'b al-Ahbar's account of a valley in Hell where the discharge of the damned gathers, into which they are plunged until their joints come apart, before being recreated and cast back into the fire, a report also cited by al-Qurtubi. Al-Razi offers a comparison: a thirsty man who drinks salty water only inflames his thirst.

Al-Qasimi and Ibn Kathir state that the mention of this punishment is itself a blessing, since it restrains from sin and encourages obedience. For this reason the passage closes with the refrain: Which of your Lord's blessings will you deny?

This verse describes the state of the wrongdoers on the Day of Judgment: they are told, as a rebuke, that this is the Hell they used to deny, and that they circulate between its fire and a boiling water, hamim an, meaning water whose heat has reached its utmost limit. The commentators agree that they are punished sometimes by the fire and sometimes by drinking this scalding liquid. Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada, Mujahid and al-Dahhak explain that an means that its heat and boiling have reached their final degree, and several cite a line of al-Nabigha, while Ibn Kathir notes that its heat is so intense it cannot be endured.

The scholars differ on how this circulation works. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi hold that they are punished by alternating between being burned in the fire and drinking the hamim, and al-Zamakhshari adds that the boiling water is given to them as relief when they cry out from the fire. Ibn al-Jawzi, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir relay from Ka'b al-Ahbar that an is a valley of Hell gathering the pus of its people, into which they are plunged, in chains, until their joints are dislocated, after which God creates them anew to be thrown back into the fire. Al-Tabari also accepts the meaning of present, reported from Ibn Zayd, while Ibn Juzayy considers the meaning of extreme heat the more apparent.

On recitation, Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu Hayyan record several readings of the verb yatufun, such as yutawwifun and yutafun, which do not change the general sense of ceaseless circling. Al-Biqa'i observes that an refers to the present moment, so that the torment never ends.

The commentators explain that this verse comes within the description of the punishment of the wrongdoers on the Day of Resurrection: they are recognised by their marks, seized by the forelock and the feet, and then told that this is the Hell which they used to deny. They circulate between the fire and a boiling water, ḥamīm ānin, meaning water that has reached the utmost of its heat. Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Sa'id ibn Jubayr and al-Suddi take the word ānin to mean that its heat has reached its limit, while Ibn Zayd takes it to mean present. Qatada, as reported by al-Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir, says it has been boiling since the creation of the heavens and the earth, and Ka'b al-Ahbar describes it as a valley of Hell in which the pus of the damned gathers. As for the verse itself, al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi hold that the blessing lies in the deliverance of whoever is saved from this punishment by God's grace, and in the warning that restrains from sin, a view shared by al-Nasafi and Ibn Sa'di. Al-Razi raises the question of how such things can be called blessings and suggests that the meaning may be the warning against Hell and the promise of Paradise. The commentators agree that the verse is a rebuke addressed to both jinn and humans. None of them decides between the interpretations of ānin transmitted from the early scholars.

This verse promises two gardens to the one who fears standing before his Lord, that is, appearing before Him for judgement, and who therefore refrains from disobedience. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Mujahid explain this fear as a man who is tempted by a sin, remembers his Lord and abandons it. Ibn Abbas instead speaks of one who fears God after performing the obligations. Ibn Kathir holds that the verse is general, covering both humans and jinn, and he takes it as evidence that believing jinn enter Paradise; Ibn al-Qayyim, al-Alusi and Ibn Ashur share this reading. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi and Ibn al-Jawzi also mention that the phrase may refer to God's watchfulness over a person's deeds, and some regard the word maqam as superfluous.

The commentators differ on the identity of the two gardens. Muqatil says they are the Garden of Eden and the Garden of Bliss. Al-Hasan and Ata' say one is the reward for avoiding wrong and the other for doing right. Al-Tirmidhi takes one to be for fear of the Lord and the other for restraining desire. Al-Razi and al-Zamakhshari hold that they are two real gardens, while al-Farra' thinks it is a single garden and the dual form serves the rhyme. Ibn al-Qayyim explains at length how the first two gardens are superior to the two that follow.

As for the "branches" (afnan), al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi report that the word means varieties, following Ibn Abbas, Ibn Jubayr and Dahhak, or boughs, following Mujahid and Ikrima. Qatada takes it to mean that the gardens excel all others.

The commentators explain that this verse names the reward of the one who fears standing before his Lord for judgment, and who, out of that fear, abstains from sin and fulfils his duties: he shall be given two gardens. They differ on the meaning of the standing: Ibn 'Abbas takes it as fear after the obligations are performed, Mujahid as a person who holds back from a sin on remembering his Lord, while others understand it as God's watchful standing over His servants who records their deeds. As for the two gardens, Ibn 'Abbas and others say they are two orchards, Muqatil names them Jannat 'Adn and Jannat al-Na'im, Ibn Kathir and al-Razi take them as one for jinn and one for humans, al-Zamakhshari and al-Qurtubi as two for each believer, and some divide them between the reward for doing good and the reward for avoiding evil. There is agreement that 'afnan' means branches or kinds of growth, and that each fruit comes in two kinds, and that the gardens contain two flowing springs and brocade cushions. Ibn 'Ashur observes that the dual form may stand for plurality, to suit the verse endings. Ibn Kathir holds the verse to be general and cites Abu al-Darda', who said that one who fears his Lord does not commit adultery or theft, without resolving the differing views on the occasion of revelation.

This verse describes two gardens, for the one who fears standing before his Lord, and calls them rich in branches. The commentators differ on the meaning of the word afnan. Mujahid, Ikrima, Ata, al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj take it to mean branches, the plural of fanan, meaning long straight boughs; Ikrima adds that these are the shade of branches over the walls. Qatada reads it as the abundance and excellence of these gardens over all others. Ibn 'Abbas, Sa'id ibn Jubayr and al-Dahhak understand it as varieties, meaning the different kinds of fruit, and Ata combines both views by saying that every branch bears many kinds of fruit. Al-Zamakhshari notes that the branches are singled out because they bear leaves and fruit and cast the shade. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir consider these explanations complementary rather than contradictory. Most commentators hold that the verse is general, applying to any believer who, out of fear of God, abandons a sin, although some link its revelation to Abu Bakr. Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Ashur conclude from it that jinn too enter Paradise when they believe and are conscious of God.

This verse states that there are two gardens for the one who fears standing before his Lord, and the surah repeats the question about the blessings that jinn and humans are asked to acknowledge. The commentators agree that the two gardens are a reward for those who fear God, obey Him and refrain from disobedience, but they differ on the meaning of fear and of the station. Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid understand it as a person who intends a sin and then, remembering his standing before his Lord, abandons it, a view al-Mawardi records among others, while Ibn 'Abbas in another report takes it as one who performs the obligations after fearing God. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi note that the station may mean the Day of Reckoning or God's watchful oversight over deeds, and Ibn 'Atiyya observes that attributing the station to the Lord signals the gravity of that moment. On the number of gardens, al-Razi and Ibn Kathir hold that there are two real gardens, while al-Farra' considers them one garden with the dual form chosen to suit the verse endings, and others divide them into a reward and an added favour. Narrations, some attributed to the Prophet and some to companions, are cited by al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir, including the report of Abu al-Darda' about the adulterer and the thief. As for afnan, Ibn 'Abbas, Ikrima and others take it to mean branches or their shade, while others take it to mean varieties of fruit or abundance and excellence. There is broad agreement on flowing springs, fruits of two kinds, cushions lined with brocade, and spouses of modest gaze whom no man or jinn has touched, and Ibn Kathir and al-Qasimi judge that the first two gardens are superior to those that follow.

This verse describes one of the two gardens prepared for the one who fears standing before his Lord: in them are two flowing springs, meaning the gardens are watered by running water. The commentators differ on the identity of these two springs. Al-Hasan al-Basri, followed by Ibn Kathir, al-Nasafi and Ibn 'Atiyya, says they are al-Tasnim and al-Salsabil, both of pure water. 'Atiyya al-'Awfi says one is water that does not spoil and the other is wine, a delight for those who drink it. Ibn 'Abbas sees them as an added honour and increase granted to the people of Paradise, while al-Kalbi and others say they flow above and below, wherever their owner wishes. Al-Qurtubi also reports from Ibn 'Abbas that each spring is like the whole of worldly water many times over. Al-Alusi and Ibn 'Ashur note that the dual form may express multiplicity rather than an exact count. Ibn 'Uthaymin suggests, tentatively, that these two springs are separate from the four rivers mentioned in Surat Muhammad. Abu Bakr al-Warraq offers an allegorical reading: whoever had eyes that flowed out of fear of God will have springs flowing in Paradise. All agree on the general picture of a well-watered paradise; only the precise identity of the springs is debated.

This passage of Surah Ar-Rahman lists God's blessings addressed to both humankind and the jinn, in the context of the two gardens promised to one who fears standing before his Lord. The recurring refrain, asking which of your Lord's blessings you two deny, serves as a reminder of grace. The commentators agree that these gardens are the reward of the hereafter and that the recipient is the one who fears God, refrains from sin and performs his duties. As for the phrase maqam rabbihi, al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Baghawi understand it as the station of judgment on the Day of Resurrection, while Mujahid and al-Nakha'i take it to mean God's watch over deeds, which restrains the believer from sin. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya note that the wording highlights the gravity of that station. On the identity of the two gardens, opinions differ: Mujahid says one is for humans and the other for jinn, Muqatil names the Garden of Eden and the Garden of Bliss, while al-Razi and al-Tabari suggest one is a dwelling and the other that of the wives and servants. For dhawata afnan, Mujahid, Ikrima and al-Baghawi take it to mean branches, Ibn 'Abbas means varieties of colour, and Qatada means abundance and excellence. All agree on the flowing springs, which al-Hasan identifies as tasnim and salsabil, while 'Ata' says water and wine. The fruits are said to be two kinds, which Ibn 'Abbas explains as including every fruit known in the world, even the bitter colocynth, though sweet there. The commentators also record the debate over the linings of brocade, which Ibn Mas'ud found so precious that one may imagine the outer layer, while Sa'id ibn Jubayr declined to elaborate. Ibn 'Ashur observes that the dual form may simply denote plurality.

This part of the verse states that in these two gardens there are two kinds of every fruit, and the commentators broadly agree on the meaning of this pairing. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn al-Jawzi explain that it means two types or two varieties, and Ibn al-Jawzi reports the prevailing view that one kind is fresh and the other dried, neither being superior to the other. Ibn 'Abbas, quoted by al-Baghawi, al-Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir, says that every fruit known in this world, sweet or bitter, exists in paradise, even colocynth, which there is sweet. Al-Sam'ani also reports from Ibn 'Abbas that what is described of paradise shares with worldly things only the names. Ibn Kathir stresses that these fruits surpass anything the eye has seen or the ear has heard. Al-Qurtubi offers a comparison: the higher gardens have one kind of each fruit, these have two. Al-Razi notes that the pair is an independent quality expressing lasting perfection, and that it is mentioned after the branches because a visitor to a garden first enjoys the sight before picking fruit. Ibn 'Ashur explains that the dual form may serve as a plural or to match the rhyme, and that the word pair here means kind. Al-Jalalayn and the Muyassar tafsir simply say the two are two species.

This verse recalls the blessing of the two gardens prepared for one who fears the standing before his Lord, and the refrain returns after each blessing of the surah, asking jinn and humans which of their Lord's blessings they deny. The commentators agree that it refers to the full range of blessings of the Hereafter, both visible and hidden. According to Ibn Abbas, Mujahid and others, the two gardens are two of the gardens of Paradise, and the flowing springs and fruits of every kind within them are part of this favour. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir explain that the two kinds of every fruit are two varieties, fresh and dried according to some, or a known and a strange kind according to others.

The fear described is the fear that restrains from sin and drives one to perform the obligations. Ibn Abbas and Ibn Kathir understand the standing as the presentation before God on the Day of Resurrection, while Mujahid takes it to mean God's watchfulness over a person's deeds, and some hold that the word is included without special meaning. As for the two gardens, al-Razi and al-Qurtubi report several views: one for performing good deeds and another for abstaining from sins, one for jinn and one for humans, or one for those brought near and one for the people of the right hand.

Opinions differ on the linings and outer layers of the cushions of thick brocade. Ibn Mas'ud says that if the linings are of brocade, the outer surfaces must be even finer, Ibn Abbas leaves their nature to what God alone knows, and al-Hasan and al-Farra' hold that the linings are the outer layers. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Kathir observe that these interpretations are all compatible with one another.

The commentators explain that this verse describes the bliss of the people of Paradise who feared the standing before their Lord: they recline on cushions whose linings are of istabraq, a thick brocade, and the fruit of the two gardens hangs within reach, whether one stands, sits or lies down, with no effort or thorns. Most agree that istabraq is thick brocade and that the fruit is near at hand; al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir cite Ibn 'Abbas saying the tree lowers itself to the believer. They differ, however, on the outer surface of the cushions. Ibn Mas'ud and Abu Hurayra argue that if the linings are like this, the outer side must be far finer, while Ibn 'Abbas and Sa'id ibn Jubayr say it is hidden knowledge, and others describe it as light or fine silk. Al-Farra' and Qatada hold that the lining and the outer face can be interchanged, a view Ibn Qutayba rejects as strange. Al-Razi and Ibn Kathir note that the mention of the lining points to the greater excellence of what is above it. On the dual 'two gardens', al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan report that each believer has two, al-Farra' suggests a single garden with the dual form for the rhyme, and al-Nahhas strongly rejects this. Overall, the commentators agree on the bliss of Paradise and the ease of reaching its fruit, but differ on the details of the cushions' outer surface and the meaning of the dual.

In this verse God addresses both humankind and the jinn, after describing the bounties of the two gardens prepared for one who fears standing before his Lord, and asks them: which of your Lord's favours will you deny? The commentators place this question at the end of the description of the couches on which the people of Paradise recline, whose linings are of istabraq, and of fruit within easy reach. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Qurtubi agree that the verse is a recurring question meant to remind the listener of the vastness of God's blessings.

The meaning of istabraq is broadly agreed: a thick brocade, according to al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi. The word batā'in, "linings", is more disputed. Qatada and Ibn Atiyya take it to mean the outer faces, citing Arab usage in which the visible side of the sky is called its back; al-Kalbi, al-Mubarrad and most others understand the inner lining itself. Ibn Qutayba rejected this usage, while al-Razi argues that mentioning only the linings shows the great nobility of the visible faces.

The commentators also report sayings attributed to Ibn Mas'ud, Abu Hurayra and Ibn Abbas, that the outer faces are beyond human knowledge, and Ibn Abbas cites the verse "no soul knows what is hidden for them of comfort to the eyes". The verse itself is therefore a reminder of these favours, and the commentators do not dispute its wording or its purpose.

This verse describes the companions of Paradise, who keep their gaze fixed on their husbands and whom no human or jinn has touched before them. The commentators agree on the general meaning: Ibn Abbas, Qatada, Mujahid and Ibn Zayd explain that they look only at their husbands, and Ibn Kathir reports that such a wife says to her husband that she sees nothing more beautiful than him in Paradise. The verb 'yatmithhunna' has several readings: al-Farra' and al-Tabari take it as deflowering and intercourse, linked to blood, while Abu 'Ubayda reads it as simple touch and al-Mubarrad as subduing. On who these women are, Muqatil says they were created in Paradise, al-Sha'bi that they are women of this world re-created, and Ata' reports from Ibn Abbas that they are believing women who died as virgins. Al-Hasan al-Basri takes them to be believing human women. Several scholars, including al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir, cite the verse to show that believing jinn enter Paradise and have wives there, while others, including Abu Hanifa, held differing views on the fate of the jinn. Al-Razi, al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi take the pronoun 'fihinna' to refer to the two gardens, while al-Farra' and others relate it to the cushions. Ibn Ashur and Ibn Sa'di stress the modesty and chastity of these women.

This verse belongs to the refrain of Surah Ar-Rahman. After describing the two gardens, their fruits, and the couches and companions within them, God asks jinn and humans which of His favours they deny. The commentators generally agree that the question refers to the blessings of Paradise just listed. On the phrase describing women who restrain their gaze, al-Tabari, Mujahid and Qatada explain that they look only at their husbands, while Ibn Abbas, Ibn Zayd and Ibn Kathir add that they find no one more beautiful than their spouse. The phrase 'no man or jinn has touched them before' is read by Ibn Abbas, Ali, Ikrima and most scholars as a reference to deflowering or intercourse, whereas Abu Ubayda and al-Mubarrad give the verb the sense of touching or taming. Several scholars, including al-Tabari, al-Qurtubi and Ibn Juzayy, take this as evidence that believing jinn enter Paradise and have spouses there, while al-Sam'ani reports the opposing views, including the claim that jinn have no reward beyond escaping the Fire. Al-Razi explains the choice of wording as a matter of modesty in speaking of intimacy. The comparison with ruby and coral is interpreted by Qatada and Ibn Kathir as the clarity of ruby and the whiteness of coral, and several hadiths describe the skin shining through layers of garments. The refrain then recurs to affirm that these blessings cannot be denied.

This verse describes the women of Paradise, whose beauty is compared to the ruby and the coral. The commentators agree on the core meaning: their radiance is like the ruby in clearness and the coral in whiteness. Qatada, al-Hasan, Mujahid and Ibn Zayd explain that they have the clearness of the ruby and the whiteness of pearls, and Ibn Kathir takes the marjan here to mean pearls. Al-Razi gives two readings of the comparison, one based on transparency and one on the whiteness of pearl and the redness of ruby, and links the verse to the phrase about women who restrain their gaze, joining chastity with beauty. Al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan note that small pearls are whiter than large ones, while Ibn 'Atiyya explains that these gems were chosen because people delight in their lustre. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and others cite the hadith of Ibn Mas'ud about seeing the marrow of the leg through seventy garments; Ibn Kathir reports it in both a raised and a stopped form and says the stopped form is sounder. Al-Tabari and al-Qurtubi take the verse to show that jinn also enter Paradise and have spouses, while others restrict the denial of touching to certain cases. The overall meaning is thus dazzling beauty joined with purity.

This passage of Surat ar-Rahman describes the delights of Paradise mentioned earlier and repeats the refrain of the surah: "Which of the favours of your Lord will you two deny?", addressed to both humans and jinn. The commentators explain that the beauty of the heavenly companions, compared to ruby and coral, means the clarity of the ruby and the whiteness of the coral. Al-Tabari, Mujahid, al-Hasan, Qatada and Ibn Zayd hold this meaning, and Ibn Kathir takes the coral to mean small pearls, which are whiter than large ones. Several scholars cite a report that the leg's marrow can be seen through seventy garments; Ibn Kathir and others present it as authentic or as transmitted from Ibn Mas'ud depending on the chain, while al-Tabari and al-Qurtubi simply record it.

On the verse "Is the reward of good other than good?", most understand that good deeds in this world are rewarded with goodness in the next, as Ibn Zayd says and Ibn Kathir reports. Ibn Abbas and Ikrima take it to mean the reward for testifying that there is no god but Allah, while Muhammad ibn al-Hanafiyya and al-Hasan read it as a reward open to the righteous and the wicked alike. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi and others offer many other meanings without settling between them.

On the two further gardens, Ibn Zayd and most commentators say the first two are for those brought near and the next two for the people of the right, al-Hasan says the first are for the foremost and the later for the followers, and Ibn Abbas ranks them by nearness to God. Some report that the first pair is of gold and the second of silver.

The commentators explain that this verse follows the description of the two gardens prepared for one who fears standing before his Lord, and that its meaning is that the reward for good deeds can only be good in return, namely the recompense and kindness of the afterlife. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, Ibn al-Jawzi, al-Nasafi and Ibn Atiyya generally take the first "good" to mean the righteous deed and the second to mean the reward, and this is the reading most widely shared. Ibn Zayd understands that good done in this world is answered by good in the next. Ibn Abbas explains it as the reward of Paradise for one who testifies that there is no god but God and follows what Muhammad brought, citing a hadith from Anas, whose chain several scholars, including al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir, note is weak. Muhammad ibn al-Hanafiyya and al-Hasan hold that the phrase is general and applies to both the righteous and the wicked, the former being rewarded in the hereafter and the latter in this world. Jafar al-Sadiq links it to the forgiveness granted to the penitent. Al-Razi lists many possible readings and suggests that God's favour is the source of the good the believer does. Ibn Ashur explains that the question in negative form expresses a restriction: the true reward of good is good, while the reward of evil is evil. The Sufis cite the saying about worshipping God as if you see Him. Finally, several commentators, including al-Zamakhshari, note that the verse applies to all, and the exegetes as a whole stress its function of reminding of God's blessings.

In this verse God addresses both humans and jinn after describing the delights of the two gardens, asking them which of their Lord's favours they deny. The commentators explain that the verse affirms that the recompense for good is good, meaning that whoever did good in this life receives good and blessing in the next. They agree that the address includes both humans and jinn, and that the verse closes the description of the reward of those who fear standing before their Lord. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi report that Ibn Zayd explained it as: what is the reward of one who did good in this world, except to be treated well in the next. Ibn 'Abbas held that it refers to whoever testifies that there is no god but God, and reports from Ibn 'Umar and Anas support this. Al-Hasan and Muhammad ibn al-Hanafiyya considered the verse general, applying to both the righteous and the wicked, the latter receiving their share in this world and the former in the next. Al-Mawardi also notes that the reward of obedience is the reward itself, and according to Ja'far al-Sadiq the reward of repentance is forgiveness. Ibn Sa'di and Ibn Kathir note that the first two gardens are for the foremost, and the latter two for the believers at large. None of the commentators decides between these readings, which they regard as complementary meanings showing the breadth of God's generosity.

This verse says that beneath the two gardens already described there are two further gardens, for whoever fears standing before his Lord. The commentators agree that these are of lower rank than the first two, but they differ on the meaning of "beneath them". Ibn 'Abbas and al-Kisa'i take it to mean lower in degree and rank, Ibn Zayd to mean lower in excellence, while others read it as "in front of them" or "nearer to the Throne". Most scholars, among them Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi, hold that the first two are for the foremost, the closely brought near, and the second two for the people of the right hand, relying on a hadith narrated by Abu Musa al-Ash'ari. Some, however, distinguish them by gold, silver, ruby and emerald. Regarding "mudhamma­tan", most explain it as a green so deep that it verges on black, as Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn al-Zubayr and Qatada said, while Mujahid renders it as dark. Most take the "gushing springs" to be fountains of water, while others say they spring with musk, camphor or fruits; al-Tabari favoured water. The palm and pomegranate are singled out after "fruit" to honour them, and the repeated question "Which of your Lord's bounties will you deny?" reminds the reader of the favours and reproaches the denial.

This verse describes two further gardens, lower in rank than the first two, for those who fear the standing before their Lord, and it returns to the question addressed to both humans and jinn: which of your Lord's bounties will you deny? The commentators agree that these two gardens are inferior to the first pair in rank and merit, as Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Zayd, al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir report. They differ on the meaning of "below them": Ibn 'Abbas takes it as lower in degree, Ibn Zayd as lower in excellence, and some assign the first pair to the foremost and these to the people of the right hand, as al-Hasan and Ibn Zayd state. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi argue that the first pair is nobler, since they are described with branches and flowing springs.

The word "mudhammatan" is glossed by Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn al-Zubayr as deep green and full of water, while Mujahid renders it as black, and Ibn Kathir notes that intense green tends toward black. All agree that "nadhdhakhatan" means gushing. Al-Tabari prefers that the springs gush with water, a view also held by Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Zayd, whereas Ibn Mas'ud and Anas speak of musk and camphor or ambergris, al-Hasan of goodness and blessing, and Sa'id ibn Jubayr of various fruits.

The separate mention of the date palm and the pomegranate is explained by their excellence, as al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya and Ibn Kathir state, while others hold that they are not counted among fruits at all. The repeated rhetorical question, according to al-Biqa'i and al-Shawkani, serves to affirm the favours and to reproach denial.

This verse describes the two gardens that lie below the first two, called mudhammatan, meaning so deep green that they tend towards black. Ibn Abbas and Ibn al-Zubayr take it to mean green and well watered, Mujahid takes it to mean blackish, and Qatada takes it to mean lush and tender. Al-Tabari adopts the reading of greenness through irrigation and cites a report from Abu Ayyub al-Ansari in the same sense. Al-Wahidi, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi explain that green which reaches its peak turns towards black, and al-Qurtubi notes the Arab usage of calling a cultivated land black. Ibn Ashur sees the image as a hyperbole for the thickness of the foliage. On the rank of these gardens, most commentators, including Ibn Kathir, Ibn Ashur and al-Razi, place them after the first two. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi and Ibn Kathir consider them inferior, relying on the lesser flow of their water and the fewer kinds of fruit. Ibn Atiyya and al-Qurtubi note that the phrase min duniha can mean lower in rank or in place, and that the question remains open, since some, such as Abu Musa al-Ash'ari and Ibn Zayd, assign the first pair to the foremost and the second to the people of the right. Al-Biqa'i observes that these gardens are dominated by plants and herbs, while the first ones are dominated by trees and fruits, a view al-Alusi repeats.

This verse describes two further gardens, below the first two that were described for one who fears the standing before his Lord, and repeats the question about the blessings of the Lord that are denied. The commentators differ on the sense of "min dunihima" (below them). Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Zayd, al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir understand it as a difference of rank or excellence, the first two gardens being higher. Al-Razi takes "dun" as a spatial position or a superiority of honour, while al-Mawardi and al-Qurtubi report that the four gardens may belong to different categories of believers, the first two for those brought near and the other two for the people of the right hand, as reported from Abu Musa al-Ash'ari.

On the word "mudhammatan", the commentators largely agree that it means a green so intense that it verges on black because of abundant water, as stated by Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn al-Zubayr, al-Tabari and Qatada, though Mujahid takes it to mean black. Al-Zajjaj notes that green, when it deepens, tends toward black. For "nadakhkhatan", most say the two springs gush forth water, a meaning that al-Tabari prefers, while others speak of musk and ambergris, of fruits, or of goodness and blessing. Al-Zamakhshari points out that gushing is less than flowing, and that the first two springs flow.

The commentators also explain that the separate mention of the date palm and the pomegranate is due to their excellence, and that the modest houris kept in tents look only at their husbands. On the nature of the tents, some say they are dwellings, others tents of hollow pearl. The commentators do not detail how the gardens differ beyond what is stated.

This verse describes, in the two gardens that come after the first two, two springs that gush forth. The most common reading among the commentators is that they gush with water powerfully and never run dry: Ibn Abbas, al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Zamakhshari adopt this meaning, and al-Tabari judges it the most correct, since water is what is ordinarily associated with springs. Al-Hasan and Mujahid explain that the springs spray goodness and blessing, while Ibn Mas'ud, Anas and Sa'id ibn Jubayr speak of musk, ambergris and camphor, or of all kinds of fruit. Al-Dahhak describes them as full and never ceasing. As for comparison with the flowing springs of the first two gardens, al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Kathir consider gushing to be less than flowing, which indicates that these two gardens rank lower, whereas al-Razi holds that gushing can be stronger than flowing and that the difference lies in the direction in which the water moves. Al-Bara' ibn Azib states that the flowing springs are better. The verse belongs to a list of God's favours, followed by the repeated question that rebukes humans and jinn for denying them.

This verse describes two gushing springs in the two lower gardens, which are for those who fear the standing before their Lord, and it asks both humans and jinn which of their Lord's favours they deny. The commentators agree that the word nadkhakhatan means gushing or spouting, and that the springs spout water. Ibn Abbas, Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Ibn Zayd adopt this meaning, while al-Dahhak describes them as full and never ceasing. Al-Hasan and Ibn Abbas understand the water as goodness and blessing, and Sa'id ibn Jubayr adds that the springs spout all kinds of fruit. Ibn Mas'ud and Anas report that they spout musk, camphor and ambergris upon the friends of God. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi hold that the spouting is less than the flowing of the springs in the first two gardens, whereas Ibn Ashur sees it as a stronger projection than mere sprinkling. The scholars agree on the purpose of the verse: to enumerate blessings and rebuke those who deny them, and on the higher rank of the first two gardens, though they give different reasons for it.

This verse describes the fruits found in the two gardens of Paradise and singles out the date palm and the pomegranate for special mention. Most commentators hold that both are included among the fruits, and that naming them separately after the general term serves to show their excellence, just as Gabriel and Michael are named after the angels. Al-Tabari transmits reports, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr and others, describing the palms of Paradise: their trunks are of gold or emerald, and their dates are whiter than milk, sweeter than honey and without a stone. Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn al-Jawzi and Ibn Kathir explain that these two gardens rank below the first two, pointing to the wording of the verse and to the contrast between their descriptions. On whether the palm and pomegranate count as fruit, al-Farra' and al-Nasafi report the view that they do not, and they cite Abu Hanifa's ruling that a man who swears not to eat fruit and eats a pomegranate or a date does not break his oath, a position his two companions rejected. The verse closes with the refrain "Which of the favours of your Lord will you deny?", used to remind listeners of these blessings. Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Uthaymin stress that the fruits of Paradise are far greater than those of this world, sharing only their names.

This repeated refrain addresses both humans and jinn after the description of the two lower gardens, asking which of their Lord's blessings they deny. Most commentators, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi, hold that the date palm and the pomegranate are part of the fruits, and were mentioned separately to honour and distinguish them, as in the verse on Gabriel and Michael. Ibn Abbas and Ibn Mas'ud, as transmitted by some, held that they are not fruits, a view al-Baghawi and others consider unusual; al-Farra' notes that the Arabs classify them as fruit. Abu Hanifa ruled that someone who swears not to eat fruit and then eats a pomegranate or fresh dates does not break his oath, though his two companions disagreed. Regarding the two gardens, al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi state that they rank below the first two, and that they are dark green from abundant water, according to Ibn Abbas and Mujahid. Opinions differ on who they are for: al-Hasan links them to the foremost and the followers, while al-Razi and Ibn Kathir stress differences in rank. The good companions are described as excellent in character and beautiful in appearance, and a hadith of Umm Salama is cited to this effect, though Ibn Kathir notes weakness in its chain. The refrain repeats after each blessing to affirm the favour and rebuke those who deny it, as al-Baghawi explains.

This verse describes the women of Paradise as excellent in character and fair of face. The commentators broadly agree on the general sense: Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada and the majority, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi, understand them as pious women of good character and beautiful appearance, and al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir both cite a hadith related through Umm Salama in support. Some, including al-Qurtubi, identify them with the houris created for Paradise, while al-Hasan takes them to be virtuous women and Isma'il ibn Abi Khalid describes them as virgins. On the reading, most read "khayrat" with a lightened form, whereas Qatada, Abu Raja' and others read "khayyirat" with a doubled letter; the philologists treat the two as equivalent forms.

The epithet "maqsurat" (kept secluded) is explained by Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid as women who stay enclosed and look only at their husbands, while al-Hasan adds that they do not roam the streets. The word "khiyam" (tents) is taken by al-Tabari and others to mean dwellings; al-Mawardi, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir report hadiths describing the tent as a single hollow pearl, sixty miles high in one narration. Several scholars note that the first two gardens are for those nearest to God and the lower two for the people of the right hand, though other commentators divide the degrees differently.

In this verse, repeated after each blessing of the two gardens, God addresses both humans and jinn and asks: which of your Lord's blessings will you deny? The commentators explain that the repetition affirms the favour and rebukes those who deny it. They agree that the two gardens mentioned here are below the first two, as Ibn Kathir and Ibn Sa'di argue from the order of mention and from the qualities described, such as flowing springs versus gushing ones. Ibn Abbas holds that the four gardens are for those who fear their Lord, while Ibn Zayd divides them between the foremost in gold and the people of the right in silver. On the phrase 'good and beautiful women', al-Tabari, Qatada and Ibn Kathir take it to mean women of excellent character and fair faces, whereas al-Razi and others understand the houris. Al-Qurtubi records that scholars differ on whether the houris excel earthly women, and he reports both views without deciding. The mention of the palm and pomegranate apart from the fruits is read by some as an exclusion and by most as an honouring of these two. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Ashur connect the description 'confined in pavilions' with modesty and protection, and al-Alusi notes that the pavilion is a hollow pearl. The repetition itself is explained by al-Baghawi and al-Suyuti as emphasis and as the tying of each verse to a preceding blessing.

In this verse God describes the women of Paradise as houris, meaning with intensely white eyes set against intensely black ones, a mark of beauty, and as maqsurat, meaning secluded and protected, within tents. The commentators agree that this confinement is one of protection and honour, not of humiliation. Mujahid and others explain that they have restricted their gaze and their selves to their husbands, desiring no other. On the precise sense of maqsurat, Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, Abu al-'Aliya and al-Dahhak take it to mean women kept inside their curtained chambers and not walking the streets, while al-Tabari joins the two meanings and favours a general sense covering both restraint of the gaze and confinement of the body. As for the tents, al-Tabari and most others take them to be dwellings. Others, including 'Umar, Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn 'Abbas, report from the Prophet ﷺ that they are hollow pearls, a tent a farsakh by a farsakh. Ibn Kathir notes that these tents are not the palaces and chambers. Al-Samani and Ibn al-Qayyim compare them to the tents of the desert Arabs, and some scholars link them to the palaces. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi also retain the image of the hollow pearl. No commentator draws a legal ruling from this verse.

In Surat al-Rahman, the refrain « Then which of the favours of your Lord will you two deny? » recurs after each favour enumerated. Commentators read it as a rebuke addressed to both humans and jinn, after the reminder of God's blessings. Verse 73 follows the description of the houris, « confined in pavilions », and belongs to that description. Most exegetes see this seclusion as a mark of honour and protection rather than punishment; al-Sam'ani calls it a confinement of dignity. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi report that the pavilions are hollow pearls, sometimes vast in size, on the basis of traditions attributed to Ibn Abbas, Umar and Ibn Mas'ud. Al-Tabari notes that « khiyam » can also mean houses, and that the Arabs sometimes call women's litters khiyam. On the meaning of « maqsurat », Mujahid says they restricted their gaze to their husbands, while Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan and Abu al-Aliya describe them as kept within their chambers and not roaming the streets. Al-Tabari, Ibn Atiyya and al-Qurtubi conclude that both meanings can stand together, and Ibn Atiyya judges the second the sounder in Arabic usage. On the reading of « yatmithhunna », most read with a kasra, al-Kisa'i alternating between kasra and damma, and al-Tabari upholds the majority reading. The commentators agree on the general purpose: magnifying the greatness of the blessing and reminding the one who denies it of what God has granted.

This verse describes the maidens of Paradise, the houris who are kept in tents, white and beautiful, and who have never been touched by any human or jinn before their husbands. The commentators agree on the core meaning: these women are chaste and reserved for their spouses. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi report that the verb means to deflower or to have intercourse, and Ibn Abbas understood it so. Mujahid, cited by al-Baghawi and Abu Hayyan, adds that humans may still lie with women when the husband does not mention God, which is why the negation covers all beings. Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi note that the verse explicitly names the jinn, and Ibn Uthaymin concludes from this that believing jinn enter Paradise as well. Al-Razi links the verse to the posture of reclining on cushions, which is central to the wider description. On the recitation, the majority read the verb with a kasra on the mim, while al-Kisa'i alternated between damma and kasra, and some read with damma on both letters or with fatha. Al-Qurtubi explains that the kasra is the common dialect and that the damma is attested as a valid Arabic usage. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Ashur also highlight the sense that these women are protected and kept for their husbands. The general reading among the commentators is that these wives have been preserved exclusively for their spouses in Paradise.

In Surat al-Rahman, the refrain « Which of the favours of your Lord will you two deny? » recurs after each blessing mentioned. In this verse it follows the description of the houris secluded in tents, whom no man or jinn has touched before their spouses. The general meaning is a rebuke and an emphasis: both humans and jinn are addressed and asked to consider the blessings listed.

The commentators agree that the repetition serves to highlight each favour and to rebuke the denial. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi and Ibn Kathir link it to each preceding blessing. On the meaning of « maqsurat », al-Tabari, Mujahid and al-Mawardi take it to mean women who restrict their gaze to their husbands, while Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan and al-Qurtubi take it to mean women kept within their chambers and not roaming the streets; al-Tabari holds that the word covers both senses.

On the tents, Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Mas'ud and 'Umar describe them as hollow pearls, and Ibn Kathir cites the hadith of Abu Musa about a single hollow pearl tent sixty miles long. Al-Tabari instead gives the sense of dwellings or litters. On the reading of « yatmithunna », most readers use a kasra on the mim, while others use a damma; al-Tabari prefers the kasra as the common usage of the language.

Ibn Kathir, Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Qurtubi note that the verse addresses both humans and jinn, and Ibn 'Uthaymin concludes that believing jinn also enter Paradise.

This verse describes the bliss of the two gardens prepared for one who fears the station of his Lord: its people recline on green "rafraf" and magnificent "abqari", that is, on cushions and fine carpets. The commentators differ on the meaning of "rafraf". Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada, al-Dahhak and Ibn Zayd take it to be the canopies or the surplus draperies over the couches and carpets, al-Hasan and al-Qurazi take it to be carpets, Ibn 'Uyayna takes it to be woven rugs, Ibn Kaysan takes it to be cushions for the elbows, while Sa'id ibn Jubayr takes it to be the meadows of Paradise. For "abqari", most say it means fine tapestries or thick rugs, Mujahid says thick brocade, and others say anything exceptionally fine, a word the Arabs linked to 'Abqar, the land they believed was home to the jinn. The commentators agree on the idea of luxury and delight, and most consider the first two gardens superior to the second two, comparing their features: flowing streams against gushing springs, two kinds of every fruit against fruits and palms and pomegranates, and brocade against green cushions. Some link the first gardens to those brought near and the second to the people of the right hand, while others do not. The repeated refrain "Which of the bounties of your Lord will you deny?" is understood as a reminder of God's favours and a rebuke to those who deny them.

After describing the two first gardens of the foremost believers, this verse addresses both humans and jinn with a rhetorical question: which of your Lord's bounties do you deny? Commentators read it as a reminder rather than a real question, since no one can truly deny such favours. The refrain returns after each bounty, and Ibn 'Ashur calls it the last repeated phrase that closes the argument for God's sole bestowal of favour and sovereignty. Al-Razi reads the repetition as emphasis on varied blessings, comparing it to poets who repeat a line for different reasons.

On the phrase "reclining on green rafraf and fine 'abqari carpets", the commentators differ. Ibn 'Abbas takes rafraf as the surplus of cushions and carpets, Sa'id ibn Jubayr as the gardens of Paradise, al-Hasan as pillows, and Ibn 'Uyayna as fine rugs. For 'abqari, Ibn 'Abbas and Qatada say embroidered rugs, Mujahid says brocade, al-Hasan says remarkable carpets, and Abu 'Ubayda links it to a land where cloth is woven. Several note that the Arabs call anything excellent 'abqari.

Opinions also differ on the ranking of the two further gardens. Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Zayd, followed by Ibn Kathir and Ibn Sa'di, identify the first two gardens with those who are brought near and the latter two with the people of the right hand, the first being of gold and the second of silver according to a hadith. Al-Hasan assigns the first pair to the foremost and the second to those who follow. Al-Qasimi notes that the less elaborate descriptions of the latter two confirm their lower rank.

The commentators explain that this verse closes Surat al-Rahman by glorifying the name of God. The name of your Lord, full of majesty and generosity, is blessed and exalted. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir report that Ibn Abbas explains it as the One possessing greatness and pride, while Sa'id ibn Jubayr and others see in it a glorification of God Himself. Most understand 'name' as referring to the divine person: Ibn Juzayy, Ibn Ashur and al-Razi follow this reading, al-Razi noting that the word may also be considered redundant, as with 'face' in the verse 'the face of your Lord remains'. Ibn Ashur explains that this is an indirect expression whose force lies in affirming God's absolute greatness. The readers differ on the form: Ibn Amir and the Syrians read 'dhu al-jalal' as a qualifier of the name, while the majority reads 'dhi al-jalal' as a qualifier of the Lord. Al-Baghawi, al-Qurtubi and Abu Hayyan note this difference without choosing. On 'tabaraka', al-Tabari, al-Razi and Ibn Ashur take it to mean being blessed, lasting in goodness and greatness, while others understand it as exalted above every imperfection. As for 'al-ikram', commentators understand it as generosity toward believers and honour toward obedient servants. Ibn Kathir and Ibn Uthaymin recall the hadith encouraging the invocation of God by these attributes. The interpretations agree on God's greatness and generosity, and this verse gracefully concludes the recounting of blessings.
